## Christ references across drafted chapters

- **Seed of the Woman** — 3:15 (The protoevangelium — the first messianic prophecy in Scripture, read in Christian and Latter-day Saint traditions as foretelling Christ's eventual victory over Satan.)
- **Shiloh (messianic reading)** — 49:10 (‘The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be.’ Jewish and Christian tradition has long read the Shiloh prophecy as messianic; the messianic line will descend through Judah (Matt 1:2-3) to David and to Christ (Rev 5:5, ‘the Lion of the tribe of Juda’). The Hebrew is genuinely difficult; the translation spectrum is reported in the LangNotes.)
- **Mighty One of Jacob; Shepherd, Stone of Israel** — 49:24 (Jacob's Joseph-blessing names God as ‘the Mighty God of Jacob; from thence is the shepherd, the stone of Israel’ (49:24). The titles — Mighty One of Jacob, Shepherd, Stone of Israel — return through the OT prophets and into the NT's stone-and-shepherd Christology (Ps 118:22 / Matt 21:42; John 10:11).)

## Per-chapter highlights

### Chapter 1 — The Beginning

*status:* draft
*themes:* creation, divine-name, imago-dei

Genesis 1 is the patterned, liturgical opening of Scripture — God speaks order out of formlessness across six days, each shaped by the rhythm "And God said... and it was so... and God saw that it was good." Humanity arrives last, made in God's image and given dominion, before the whole movement comes to rest on the seventh day.

### Chapter 2 — The Garden of Eden

*status:* draft
*themes:* creation, imago-dei, marriage

Genesis 2 narrows from the cosmic creation of Genesis 1 to a focused account of humanity in the garden. God forms the man from the dust of the ground — *adam* from *adamah* — breathes into him the breath of life, plants a garden in Eden and places the man in it to keep it, then forms woman from his side as a "helper corresponding to him." The chapter sets in place the foundational scriptural vocabulary for sacred space, work, marriage, and the human relationship with the earth.

### Chapter 3 — The Fall and the First Promise

*status:* draft
*themes:* fall, atonement, messianic-prophecy

Genesis 3 is the pivot of primeval history: the serpent's deception, the eating of the forbidden fruit, divine confrontation in the cool of the day, the curses, and the expulsion from Eden — all in twenty-four verses. Yet at the chapter's center stands the protoevangelium, the first promise of a coming Deliverer: the seed of the woman who will bruise the serpent's head. The human condition the rest of Scripture responds to is set in place here, alongside the first hint of the Atonement that will answer it.

### Chapter 4 — Cain and Abel

*status:* draft
*themes:* fall, atonement

Genesis 4 follows the first family beyond Eden into the consequences of the Fall: two brothers, two offerings, two responses from God — and then the first murder. Cain's curse, the merciful mark, and his exile open into a brief account of his civilization-building lineage, and Lamech's vengeance song shows how quickly sin compounds. The chapter closes with the birth of Seth as the appointed continuation of the righteous line, and the note that "then began men to call upon the name of the Lord."

### Chapter 5 — From Adam to Noah

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, prophetic-call, restoration

Genesis 5 traces ten generations from Adam to Noah in a careful genealogical structure marked by the formula *toledoth* — Genesis's structural divider that returns throughout the book. The long lifespans give the chapter its distinctive feel, but its theological pivot is Enoch: "And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him." From those two verses the Pearl of Great Price expands a full prophetic biography — Enoch's call, his vision of cosmic history, and the founding of the city of Zion — that the Genesis text leaves almost entirely implicit.

### Chapter 6 — The Sons of God, the Nephilim, and the Ark

*status:* draft
*themes:* judgment, prophetic-call

Genesis 6 narrates a pre-flood corruption so total that "every imagination of the thoughts of [the human] heart was only evil continually." The chapter opens with the cryptic passage about "sons of God" and "daughters of men" producing the Nephilim, then narrows to the divine grief, the resolution to cleanse the earth, and the contrasting note of Noah's righteousness. By the chapter's end God has given Noah the dimensions for the ark and the promise of a covenant — the first explicit mention of *berith* in Genesis.

### Chapter 7 — The Flood Comes

*status:* draft
*themes:* judgment, salvation

Genesis 7 brings the warning of chapter 6 to its catastrophic answer. Noah, his family, and the animals enter the ark; seven days later "the fountains of the great deep [are] broken up, and the windows of heaven [are] opened." The rain falls forty days; the waters prevail over the earth a hundred and fifty; every living thing on dry land outside the ark dies. The chapter is the world's near-undoing — the chaos of Genesis 1:2 returning, briefly, to swallow the order that had been spoken into place.

### Chapter 8 — The Waters Recede

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration

Genesis 8 turns the flood narrative back toward life: "And God remembered Noah," and the waters begin to recede. The ark rests on the mountains of Ararat; the raven and dove are sent out; Noah disembarks onto a remade earth and builds the first altar in Scripture. The Lord's heart turns — "I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake" — and the chapter ends in a quiet covenant promise that while the earth remaineth, the seasons will not cease.

### Chapter 9 — The Noahic Covenant

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration, imago-dei

Genesis 9 establishes the first explicit *berith* (covenant) in Scripture — God's promise to Noah, his descendants, and "every living creature" that the waters will never again destroy all flesh, with the rainbow set in the cloud as the sign. The chapter renews the creation blessing, reasserts the imago Dei as the basis for the prohibition on murder, and gives the first dietary regulations. A closing scene of Noah's drunkenness and his prophetic word over his sons has been read carefully ever since — including in places, sadly, where it has been read wrongly.

### Chapter 10 — The Table of Nations

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, kingdom-of-god

Genesis 10 maps the post-flood human family across seventy descendants of Noah's three sons — Japheth, Ham, and Shem — and the peoples and territories that take their names. The chapter is the only sustained catalogue of nations in early Scripture, and its theological work is to establish the universalism against which the Abrahamic call of chapter 12 will be set. The only named figure given narrative depth is Nimrod, "a mighty hunter before the Lord," whose kingdom includes Babel — preparing the chapter that follows.

### Chapter 11 — Babel and the Line to Abraham

*status:* draft
*themes:* judgment, covenant

Genesis 11 closes the primeval history: the tower of Babel — humanity unified in ambition to "make us a name" — meets the divine confusion of language and the scattering that the Table of Nations in Genesis 10 has already mapped. Then the chapter pivots, in a focused genealogy of Shem leading to Terah, then to Abram and Sarai, and the migration from Ur of the Chaldees to Haran. The chapter is the funnel from universal humanity to the one family through whom blessing will reach every nation — and the threshold of the patriarchal narrative that the rest of Genesis will tell.

### Chapter 42 — Joseph's Brothers Go to Egypt

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, faith

The famine drives Jacob to send ten sons to Egypt for grain; they bow before Joseph with their faces to the earth, and Joseph remembers his boyhood dreams. Hiding his identity, he accuses them of espionage, holds Simeon as hostage, and demands they bring Benjamin — and they confess to one another, not knowing he understands, that this trouble has come because of their brother. Joseph weeps, restores the money secretly to their sacks, and Jacob refuses to part with Benjamin: "all these things are against me."

### Chapter 43 — The Second Journey, with Benjamin

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, faith

The famine forces the issue. Judah, taking the lead his brothers cannot, pledges himself as surety for Benjamin, and Jacob at last releases the youngest along with double money and a present of the best of the land. The brothers come again to Joseph; he asks after his father, sees Benjamin, withdraws to weep, and seats them at his table in birth-order — to their astonishment — with Benjamin's portion five times any other's.

### Chapter 44 — The Silver Cup; Judah's Plea

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, faith, atonement

Joseph commands his steward to plant his silver cup in Benjamin's sack; the brothers depart, are overtaken, the cup is found, and they return in dread to Joseph's house. Judah rises and gives the longest speech of the patriarchal narratives — recounting the family's history, naming his own pledge of surety, and at last offering himself in Benjamin's place: "let thy servant abide instead of the lad a bondman to my lord; and let the lad go up with his brethren." The substitutionary plea is the climax of the testing.

### Chapter 45 — Joseph Reveals Himself

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, faith, restoration

Joseph can refrain himself no longer; he sends all the Egyptians out, weeps so loudly the household hears him, and says, "I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?" To his terrified brothers he speaks the providence theology that defines the chapter — "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good" — and sends them home to bring Jacob to Egypt. Pharaoh confirms the invitation; Joseph sends wagons and gifts; the brothers tell Jacob "Joseph is yet alive," and the spirit of Jacob their father revives.

### Chapter 46 — Jacob Migrates to Egypt

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, faith, prophetic-call

Jacob travels with all his household to Beersheba and offers sacrifices, and God speaks to him in the night: "Fear not to go down into Egypt; for I will there make of thee a great nation: I will go down with thee... and I will also surely bring thee up again." Genesis lists the seventy souls who went down into Egypt — the seed of the nation the Exodus will deliver. At Goshen Joseph meets his father; they fall on each other's necks and weep a long while; Jacob's first words: "Now let me die, since I have seen thy face."

### Chapter 47 — Jacob Before Pharaoh; the Famine

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, faith

Joseph presents five of his brothers and Jacob to Pharaoh; the family is settled in Goshen, and Jacob — the wandering patriarch — blesses Pharaoh and names his life "few and evil... an hundred and thirty years." Joseph administers the famine, gathering all the money, then the cattle, then the land of Egypt into Pharaoh's hand on a one-fifth perpetual share. Jacob, near death, makes Joseph swear to bury him not in Egypt but with his fathers in Canaan.

### Chapter 48 — Jacob Blesses Ephraim and Manasseh

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, faith

Joseph brings his two Egyptian-born sons to the dying Jacob; Jacob recounts the Bethel theophany, adopts Ephraim and Manasseh as his own ("they shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon"), and blesses them with crossed hands — the right on Ephraim the younger, the left on Manasseh the elder. Joseph protests the inversion; Jacob: "I know it, my son, I know it... his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations" — and the God-who-fed-me and the Angel-who-redeemed-me are invoked over the boys.

### Chapter 49 — Jacob Blesses the Twelve Tribes

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, messianic-prophecy, prophetic-call, judgment

Jacob gathers his twelve sons and speaks the longest sustained poetic oracle of Genesis — the destiny of each tribe in turn. Reuben forfeits the firstborn dignity; Simeon and Levi are scattered for Shechem's violence; Judah receives the sceptre with the Shiloh prophecy that Jewish and Christian tradition has read as messianic; Joseph receives the blessings of heaven, deep, and womb. The twelve tribes of Israel — and the messianic line through Judah — are set on their trajectories in 27 verses.
